issue: RAG /search opens a brand-new Postgres connection (new pg.Client) and tears it down (client.end()) on EVERY search_project_docs call instead of using a pooled connection.
evidence: const client = new pg.Client(DB_CONFIG); ... await client.connect(); ... } finally { await client.end(); }
estimated_impact: TCP + TLS + Postgres auth handshake on every query: ~20-60ms added p50 per /search on top of the embedding+vector cost; under bursty agent traffic this also risks connection churn and ephemeral-port/backend-slot exhaustion. With pg.Pool the handshake is amortized to ~0ms after warmup.
recommendation: Create a single module-scope pg.Pool once at startup and call pool.query(sql, params) per request; never connect/end per call. Keep it open for the process lifetime (stdio MCP server is long-lived).

issue: RAG /search creates a fresh OpenAI client and re-embeds the query text on every call with no caching of identical/recent queries; embeddings for repeated queries are recomputed.
evidence: const openai = new OpenAI({ apiKey }); ... embedding = await embedText(query, openai);
estimated_impact: Each embedText call is a network round-trip to OpenAI (~100-400ms p50, billed per token). Agents frequently issue near-identical queries; a small LRU cache keyed on the normalized query would cut p50 by the full embedding latency (100-400ms) on cache hits and reduce API spend.
recommendation: Instantiate the OpenAI client once at module scope. Add a bounded LRU (e.g. 500 entries) cache mapping normalized query -> embedding vector. Consider also caching the final result rows for hot queries with a short TTL.

issue: Feature-flag reads call fs.readFileSync + JSON.parse on the request thread on EVERY GET. The copilot-instructions list feature-flag reads as a known hot path.
evidence: function loadFeatures() { const raw = readFileSync(FEATURES_PATH, 'utf-8'); return JSON.parse(raw) } ... getFeatureFlags / getFeatureFlagByName call loadFeatures() per request
estimated_impact: Synchronous disk read (~14KB features.json) blocks the Node event loop on every feature-flag request, stalling all concurrent requests for the duration of the read+parse (~0.5-2ms each, worse under disk contention). At high RPS this serializes the whole event loop. Quantify: 14KB parse ~0.3-1ms event-loop block per call x every flag read.
recommendation: Load features.json once into a module-scope variable at startup; on update (writeFileSync) refresh the in-memory copy. Or use fs.promises.readFile + await to at least avoid blocking, but caching in memory is the real fix for a read-hot, write-rare file.

issue: Every MCP feature-flag tool call (list_features, get_feature_info, set_feature_state, adjust_traffic_rollout) does a synchronous readFileSync + JSON.parse of features.json; writes use synchronous writeFileSync.
evidence: function loadFeatures(): FeaturesDB { const raw = readFileSync(DATA_PATH, 'utf-8'); return JSON.parse(raw) } ... loadFeatures() called at the top of all four tools
estimated_impact: Blocks the MCP server event loop per tool call (~0.3-1ms for the 14KB file). Lower volume than the HTTP path so medium, but identical anti-pattern; readFileSync on a read-mostly file is avoidable.
recommendation: Cache the parsed DB in memory; re-read only after a save (or watch the file). Use fs.promises for the write to avoid blocking on the slower write path.

issue: getOrders (GET /api/orders, admin order list) returns ALL orders with no limit/skip and populates user on each — unbounded result set on a known hot path.
evidence: const orders = await Order.find({}).populate('user', 'id name'); res.json(orders)
estimated_impact: Grows linearly with total orders. At 50k orders each carrying an embedded orderItems array + shipping/payment objects, the response can be many MB serialized in one synchronous JSON.stringify, holding that memory per concurrent request and adding hundreds of ms to seconds of latency + GC pressure. The .populate adds an extra batched users query (acceptable) but the missing LIMIT is the real problem.
recommendation: Add pagination (limit/skip with a pageSize, mirror getProducts) and an index-backed sort (e.g. createdAt desc). Return a paged envelope { orders, page, pages }.

issue: getMyOrders (GET /api/orders/myorders) returns all of a user's orders unbounded, no limit and no sort/index.
evidence: const orders = await Order.find({ user: req.user._id }); res.json(orders)
estimated_impact: Bounded per-user but heavy users / long-lived accounts accumulate large order histories; full collection scan on { user } without an index (see PERF-010) plus unbounded payload. Tens of ms to hundreds as histories grow.
recommendation: Paginate and add an index on Order.user (and sort by createdAt). Limit default page size.

issue: getUsers (GET /api/users, admin user list) returns ALL users with no pagination AND includes the bcrypt password hash field (no .select('-password')).
estimated_impact: Unbounded payload that grows with the user base; on 100k+ users this is a multi-MB response + large synchronous serialization blocking the event loop. Also leaks password hashes (cross-ref security-review — exposure/over-fetch). Perf cost scales linearly with user count.
recommendation: Add pagination (limit/skip) and .select('-password'). Sort by an indexed field.

issue: getTopProducts (GET /api/products/top) runs Product.find({}).sort({ rating: -1 }).limit(3) on every homepage carousel load with no caching and no index on rating — an in-memory sort of the whole collection.
estimated_impact: Without an index on rating, MongoDB must scan all products and sort in memory on every carousel render (every homepage hit). At 100k products that is a full COLLSCAN + SORT (>100ms, blocking that connection) for a result that changes rarely. The carousel polls/renders on every home visit.
recommendation: Add an index on { rating: -1 } so the sort is index-backed, and cache the top-3 result in memory with a short TTL (e.g. 60s) since it is low-cardinality and changes infrequently. Add Cache-Control/ETag on the response.

issue: No HTTP caching headers (Cache-Control / ETag) on cacheable public GET endpoints (/api/products, /api/products/top, /api/feature-flags, /api/config/paypal) and no compression middleware.
evidence: app.use('/api/products', productRoutes) ... app.get('/api/config/paypal', ...) — no compression(), no cache headers anywhere
estimated_impact: Every product-list / top / config request hits Mongo and ships uncompressed JSON. Adding gzip/br compression typically cuts JSON payload 60-80% (faster TTFB on 3G/mobile, lower egress). Cache-Control on the largely-static catalog and paypal config would let browsers/CDN skip the origin entirely.
recommendation: Add the compression middleware and set Cache-Control (e.g. public, max-age=60) + ETag on read-only catalog endpoints; cache /api/config/paypal aggressively (it is a static client id).

issue: Order.user has no index though it is the filter key for getMyOrders ({ user: req.user._id }); Product has no index on the search field name or on rating used by getTopProducts.
evidence: user: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, required: true, ref: 'User' } — no `index: true`; productModel has no index on name or rating
estimated_impact: Order.find({ user }) and the top-products sort do full collection scans. On 1M-row collections an unindexed equality/sort query is +500ms to 2s per query vs a few ms with an index. Scales with collection growth.
recommendation: Add index: true on Order.user (compound { user: 1, createdAt: -1 } for the paged myorders query), an index on Product.rating: -1 for getTopProducts, and a text index (or index on name) for the product search regex.

issue: Product search uses a case-insensitive unanchored $regex on user input for the keyword filter; even though the special chars are escaped (ReDoS mitigated per security-review), an unanchored /i regex cannot use a standard index and forces a collection scan + per-document regex evaluation.
estimated_impact: Every keyword search is a full COLLSCAN with regex applied to each product name. On large catalogs this is the dominant search cost (linear in product count, +100ms-1s as catalog grows). Also the countDocuments + find run sequentially (two scans per search).
recommendation: Use a MongoDB $text index with $text/$search (index-backed, far faster) or at least an anchored prefix regex with a collation index. Consider running count and find concurrently (Promise.all) since they are independent.

issue: getProducts issues countDocuments and find sequentially with two awaits; they are independent and could run concurrently.
evidence: const count = await Product.countDocuments({ ...keyword }); const products = await Product.find({ ...keyword }).limit(pageSize).skip(...)
estimated_impact: Two sequential DB round-trips per product-list request. Running them with Promise.all roughly halves the DB wait on this hot path (saves ~one round-trip, ~5-30ms depending on regex/scan cost).

issue: All 17 route screens are statically imported into App.jsx — no React.lazy / dynamic import / code splitting. Heavy admin-only screens (FeatureDashboard, lists, edit screens) and the PayPal-button screen ship in the initial bundle for every visitor.
evidence: import HomeScreen ... import OrderScreen ... import FeatureDashboardScreen from './screens/FeatureDashboardScreen'; — all eager, then plain <Route component=...> with no lazy/Suspense
estimated_impact: First paint downloads JS for admin dashboards and screens a typical shopper never visits, inflating the initial bundle and LCP/TTI. Code-splitting the admin + checkout routes commonly trims 100-300KB from the entry chunk = roughly +200-600ms LCP saved on 3G/mobile.
recommendation: Wrap route screens (especially admin/*, OrderScreen with PayPal) in React.lazy + <Suspense> so they load on demand.

issue: react-paypal-button-v2 is statically imported into OrderScreen, and the PayPal SDK script is injected on mount; combined with no code-splitting (PERF-013) the PayPal client lib is in the bundle even for users who never reach checkout.
estimated_impact: react-paypal-button-v2 pulls in a sizeable dependency tree; bundling it globally adds to every page's JS. Lazy-loading the order/checkout route removes it from the critical path (tens to ~100+KB).
recommendation: Lazy-load OrderScreen (and thus PayPalButton) via React.lazy; the SDK <script> injection is already deferred which is good — keep that pattern.

issue: OrderScreen mutates and recomputes order.itemsPrice via reduce in the component body on every render (not memoized), mutating the Redux-store object in place.
estimated_impact: Cheap per item but runs on every render and mutates store state (anti-pattern that can cause subtle re-render/stale issues). Negligible CPU for small carts; flagged as hygiene.
recommendation: Compute itemsPrice in a useMemo over order.orderItems, or derive it in the reducer/selector instead of mutating the store object during render.

issue: Product grid images have no explicit width/height, no loading="lazy", and are unsized originals served from /uploads — list grids of many products load all full-size images eagerly.
evidence: (no width/height/loading attributes)
estimated_impact: Missing intrinsic dimensions => CLS (layout shift) as images load; eager-loading every grid image hurts LCP and wastes bandwidth on offscreen cards. Cross-ref: uploads are unbounded in size (security-review upload finding), so a large uploaded image directly degrades LCP/bandwidth.
recommendation: Add width/height (or aspect-ratio) and loading="lazy" to grid images; serve resized/optimized variants. Enforcing an upload size limit (security finding) caps the worst case.

issue: createProductReview loads the entire product (including the full embedded reviews array) and recomputes rating by re-reducing ALL reviews on each new review; the reviews array is an unbounded embedded subdocument array.
evidence: const product = await Product.findById(...); product.reviews.push(review); product.rating = product.reviews.reduce(...) / product.reviews.length; await product.save()
estimated_impact: For very popular products the reviews array grows unbounded inside the product document (Mongo 16MB doc cap, and every product fetch ships all reviews). Re-reducing all reviews per write is O(n) but minor; the unbounded embedded growth is the real concern — it inflates getProductById payloads and product-list memory over time.
recommendation: Consider moving reviews to a separate collection (paginated) for high-volume products, or cap/paginate embedded reviews; maintain rating via incremental average ((rating*numReviews+new)/(numReviews+1)) instead of re-reducing.

note: No classic ORM-in-loop N+1 found. Order/user populates use Mongoose .populate (batched $in), not per-item findById. The closest issues are missing pagination/indexes (PERF-005/006/007/010) and per-call connection setup in the RAG server (PERF-001). MCP feature-flag dependency resolution (resolveDependencies) reads from the already-loaded in-memory db object, not per-dep DB calls — fine.
